props.text: The full surgical procedure, with muscle repair and skin removal, for a neck that has gone past what a suture can hold.
$18,000 with the face, planned and performed together
A neck lift is not a skin operation.
Three layers have changed and a result that lasts means addressing all three in the same sitting. The one people expect to hear about is the one nearest the surface, and it is the least of them.
The sheet of muscle that gives the neck its shape, repaired where it has separated. This is the layer that holds, and it is the reason a neck lift lasts longer than anything that only tightens skin.
Where the muscle is lax but the skin still has tone, a suture suspension may be enough on its own. That is the MyEllevate
conversation, and it is a cheaper and shorter one.
Contoured where it has accumulated under the chin and along the jaw, so that the border the muscle repair creates has a clean line to sit against rather than a soft one.
Fullness under the chin is sometimes fat rather than muscle, and sometimes both. Which it is on you is measured at the consultation, not guessed at from a photograph.
Removed where it is genuinely in excess, rather than redraped over the problem. Treating the skin as the problem is how a neck ends up looking operated on rather than rested.
Skin is the last layer and the one everybody names first. A procedure that only pulls it tight is why work that has been done looks done.
The test is whether the skin takes up when you lift your chin.
This is the operation when there is real skin excess. If the skin retracts when the chin is raised, a suspension procedure may still be enough. If it hangs, it needs removing.

Loose skin that does not take up when the chin is raised

pages.seoDescription: Eyelid surgery, upper or lower, by Dr. Mona Stone. An hour or less in the chair and seven to ten days off work. $3,400 in Westlake, TX.

props.text: Eyelid surgery, upper or lower. The smallest operation on this list and, for most faces, the one that changes the most.
Upper or lower, as the practice's own price list quotes it
Three tissues, and the skin is only the first of them.

The practice describes the upper lid operation in a single sentence: excess skin, muscle and fat, removed and repositioned. Most people arrive believing it is the first of those three, and the part that actually changes how an eye reads is usually the last.

The fat that sits behind the muscle and pushes forward as the tissue holding it back gives way. It is what a bag under the eye is made of, and it is why bags are there the moment you wake rather than only after a bad night.
Modern technique is increasingly about repositioning this fat into the hollow beneath the eye rather than removing it. Taking it out is how a lid ends up looking hollow instead of rested.
A strip of the muscle that circles the eye is addressed where it is contributing to the fold, at the same time and through the same opening as the skin above it.
This is the layer nobody asks about and the reason two lids that had the same amount of skin taken off can settle differently.

The fold that has come to sit on the crease, or on the lashes, or in marked cases into the outer field of vision. It is the layer everybody names first and the easiest of the three to judge in a mirror.
It is also the layer that punishes over-resection hardest on the lower lid. Take too much and the lid pulls away from the eye, which is difficult to correct and immediately obvious.
The test is what happens when the brow is held where it used to sit.

Lift the skin at the tail of your brow with a fingertip. If that single millimetre opens the eye and softens the expression, your operation is a brow lift and not this one. If the eye stays heavy with the brow held up, the weight is in the lid itself, and that is what this page is about.
Which of these sound like you?
Upper lid skin that folds over the crease, or sits on the lashes
Bags or puffiness that are there the moment you wake, rather than after a bad night
Hollowing beneath the eye that makes the cheek and the lid read as two separate structures
Eye makeup that will no longer sit on the upper lid because there is nowhere flat for it to go
Tick whichever apply. Nothing here is stored or sent.

props.text: Where the real problem is a descended brow resting on the lid, the answer is a brow and forehead lift at $5,000–7,000, and taking lid skin instead would be the wrong operation done well. Dr. Stone will hold your brow in position at the consultation and show you the difference rather than describe it.
In the crease above, and beneath the lash line below.

On the upper lid the incision is made where the skin naturally folds, so the scar sits in the crease and disappears into it once healed. Excess skin, muscle and fat are removed or repositioned through that one opening.

On the lower lid the incision goes just beneath the lash line, or inside the lid entirely where only fat is being addressed, in which case there is no external scar at all. Which of the two is used depends on whether skin needs removing or only fat needs moving.

It is an outpatient operation and it typically takes an hour or less. Local anaesthetic is used, with sedation or a general where the work or the patient calls for it. The practice uses a long-acting local that can carry pain relief for forty to seventy two hours afterwards, which is why most patients need nothing stronger at home, and you can choose to have a platelet rich plasma or platelet rich fibrin treatment during the procedure to help the site heal.
A morning, a week of bruising, and a lid that keeps settling.

This is the shortest recovery of any operation on the practice's surgical list. The figures below are its conventional ranges and they are what to plan around; Dr. Stone will give you the numbers for your own lids at the consultation.
An hour or less, and home the same day

One to two hours if both upper and lower lids are being done together. You go home the same day, and somebody else drives: sedation rules that out for you for twenty four hours whatever you feel like.

Bruising is the main event and it is worst around days two and three. Cold compresses and sleeping propped up shorten it considerably. Expect tenderness, watering, light sensitivity and some blurring from the ointment, all of which are on the practice's own list of what is normal.

At around a week. Most of the healing happens inside the first fortnight and most people are back to normal activities inside it, which is what makes this the operation people fit around a job rather than the other way round.
Comfortable in company, then in photographs

Most people are comfortable in company at ten days and in photographs at three weeks. The last of the swelling in the lid resolves over two to three months, and the scar in the crease keeps fading well past that.
The bruising week is at home, and it is a week.
By three weeks most people have stopped avoiding cameras.
Three different answers to "something about my eyes".

These are not three sizes of the same operation. One works above the eye, one works on the lid, and one works on the surface of the skin, and it is common to need two of them. Which is which is decided at the consultation and each is quoted separately.

Morpheus8 does related work sub-dermally, usually across one to three sessions. Chemical peels lift the top layers so newer skin comes up. Financing, and a membership that banks what you don’t spend.

The practice finances through Sunbit, an application that takes about a minute and does not affect your credit score to check, and also works with CareCredit and Scratchpay. For ongoing treatment rather than a one-off procedure, a membership is usually the cheaper route: the monthly amount becomes credit that accumulates instead of expiring.
The comparisons people get stuck on.
or a neck lift: how do I know which?
A neck lift uses small incisions behind the ears and under the chin to reach the tissue underneath, and delivers a result that can last up to ten years. MyEllevate
places internal sutures through small punctures instead, and lasts around five. MyEllevate
suits earlier laxity; a neck lift reverses more advanced sagging, wrinkling or fullness. It is also a practical difference on the day: MyEllevate
needs only local anaesthetic, so you can drive yourself home.
Will a neck lift fix my jowls?

No, and this is the most common mix-up. Jowls sit low on the face, so people assume they are neck work, but they originate in sagging facial tissue and are addressed in a facelift, not a neck lift. A minimally invasive facelift is the procedure that reduces them.

Fillers are gel injectables that plump and smooth lines, acne scars and thin lips, and last from months to a couple of years depending on the product and the site. Implants are customised inserts that reshape the underlying structure and are made from a biocompatible material that stays intact, so the contour is permanent. Filler changes the surface; an implant changes the frame.
How long does each result actually last?
The practice’s own published figures: blepharoplasty 10–15 years or more; a neck lift up to ten; MyEllevate

around five; facial implants and buccal fat reduction permanent, though significant weight gain can put fullness back into the cheek elsewhere. Injectables are months, not years, which is what makes them maintenance rather than surgery.
Can I have more than one procedure at once?

Often, and it is frequently the better plan: a neck lift can be done alongside a facelift or eyelid surgery in a single procedure, with one recovery instead of two. What can be combined safely depends on your anatomy and how long you would be under anaesthetic, so it is decided at the consultation rather than in advance.
Why do some rows say “at consultation” instead of a price?

Because the practice never published a figure for those, and we would rather show you a gap than a guess. Genioplasty, fat transfer and facelift fees genuinely vary with the case, as the practice’s own pages say. Everything else on this page carries the fee the practice published, which is being reconfirmed for 2026.

The suture does the lifting, so nothing is cut away.

Most people who come in about their neck are not asking for a facelift. They want the line under the chin back, the one that makes a jaw look like a jaw, and they cannot take three weeks off to get it. This is the procedure that sits in that gap.

A light-guided suture is passed beneath the skin and used to suspend the platysma, the sheet of muscle that gives the neck its shape. Because the suture does the lifting, there is no external incision, and because nothing is cut away, the result is a repositioning of what you already have rather than a removal.

Nothing is removed. This procedure depends on skin that still has tone, because it redrapes over the suspended muscle rather than being trimmed. Where the skin needs help of its own, FaceTite tightens it by radiofrequency in the same visit, priced together at $7,800.
Skin with genuine excess will not take up over a suture, and that is the single test that decides between this and a neck lift.
It works when the skin still takes up.

It works best where the skin still has reasonable tone and the problem is laxity in the muscle rather than a genuine excess of skin. In practice that tends to mean people in their late thirties to their fifties, and people of any age who have lost weight and been left with a slack neck.

pages.seoDescription: The full face and neck lift: the SMAS repositioned, the platysma repaired, the skin redraped rather than pulled. $18,000 in Westlake, TX, by Dr. Mona Stone.

props.text: The full procedure, face and neck addressed together, because the two age as one structure and lifting only half of it shows.
$11,000 for the neck alone, where the face has aged more slowly than the jawline
A face lift is not about pulling skin tight.

Skin is the last layer, and treating it as the problem is how a face ends up looking operated on rather than rested. The work happens underneath, in the layer of muscle and fascia that has descended, and the skin is redraped over the result rather than dragged into position.

The sheet of muscle and fascia under the skin of the face is what has descended, and it is what is lifted and fixed back where it sat. In the neck the same layer is the platysma, repaired in the midline where it has separated. This is the layer that holds, and it is why the result lasts.
Where the descent is real but the skin still has tone, the neck can sometimes be answered with a suture alone. That is the
conversation, and being pointed at it is a normal outcome here.
The fat, put back where it belongs

A jowl is fat that has slid below the jawline; a hollow cheek is fat that has left. Both are addressed with the deeper layer rather than treated as the problem on their own, and fullness under the chin is contoured through the same neck incision.
Where the mid-face has genuinely lost volume, fat transfer can be planned alongside. It is decided at the consultation, on your anatomy.

Once the deeper layer is where it belongs, the skin is laid back over it and only the genuine excess is removed. No tension is carried in the skin, which is the difference between a face that looks rested and one that looks pulled.
A lift restores position. It does not change the quality of the skin on top of it, which is what resurfacing is for, and it is often staged afterwards.
This is the operation for genuine descent and genuine excess.
Rather than early laxity that a suture suspension could still hold. It tends to be people in their fifties and sixties, and younger people who have lost a large amount of weight.

Through them the SMAS is lifted and fixed back where it sat, the platysma is repaired where it has separated, fat is contoured along the jaw and under the chin, and the skin is redraped over the result with only the genuine excess removed.

The six questions this operation raises.
Where do the scars go, and will people see them?

They follow the natural creases in front of the ear, around the earlobe and back into the hairline behind it. They are placed where the anatomy hides them and they mature over months from pink to pale. Scar care starts as soon as the wounds are closed and is part of your plan, not an afterthought.

A well-executed lift resets the clock rather than stopping it. Most people look substantially better than their unoperated baseline for a decade or more, and you continue to age normally from the new starting point. Skin quality, weight stability, sun exposure and genetics all move that figure, and Dr. Stone will give you a realistic number for your face rather than an average.
Will I look like a different person?

No, and if a result looks like a different person then something has gone wrong with the planning. The aim is that people register that you look well rather than that you look altered. That is a matter of how much tension is placed on which layer, and it is decided in the operating theatre rather than promised beforehand.

Can I combine it with eyelid surgery or resurfacing?
